common_name: Kakoden Peony (Historic Japanese Double White Herbaceous Peony, Itoh Seed Parent)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Kakoden is an old Japanese double-flowered herbaceous peony, long grown in the Nagano region, bearing fragrant, bowl-shaped white to pale blush flowers over red-mottled stems on an upright plant. Its chief claim to horticultural fame is as the herbaceous seed parent Toichi Ito used in the 1940s when he crossed it with the Lemoine tree peony hybrid 'Alice Harding,' producing the first successful intersectional crosses and founding the entire Itoh class of peonies, including early cultivars such as Yellow Crown, Yellow Emperor, and Yellow Heaven. On its own it performs as a reliable, fully herbaceous garden peony, dying back completely each winter rather than showing any of the shrubby persistence seen in its intersectional offspring. Grow in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and leave the crown undisturbed once established to build toward its fullest bloom over several seasons.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society), Paeonia Itoh Cultivars

common_name: Alice Harding Tree Peony (Lemoine Yellow Double Lutea-Hybrid Tree Peony, Itoh Pollen Parent)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade.

directions: Alice Harding is a French lutea-hybrid tree peony raised by the Lemoine nursery and introduced in 1935, one of the first double yellow tree peonies, carrying fully double, lemon-yellow, sweetly scented flowers on a low, woody bush that holds its shape as a permanent shrub rather than dying back in winter. It was bred from Paeonia lutea crossed with a double Paeonia suffruticosa cultivar, part of the same lutea-hybrid breeding line that later produced cultivars like Golden Era. Its chief historical significance beyond the garden is as the woody pollen parent Toichi Ito crossed onto the herbaceous cultivar Kakoden in the 1940s, a union that produced the first Itoh intersectional peonies and launched an entirely new class of hybrids. Plant in a permanent site in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, giving full sun in cooler climates and afternoon shade where summers are hot, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society), Paeonia Itoh Cultivars

common_name: Martha W. Peony (Wisconsin Light Pink Lactiflora, Proven Itoh Seed Parent)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Martha W. is a Wisconsin chance seedling of unknown parentage, possibly related to 'Mons. Jules Elie,' found and registered by Spangler in 1985, bearing single light-pink flowers in early to midseason on tall, stiff, wiry stems without fragrance. Its real significance lies outside the show bench: breeders discovered it to be an unusually fertile seed parent for intersectional crosses, setting abundant large seed when pollinated with tree peonies, which made it a workhorse parent behind several Itoh hybrids, including Don Smith's 'Berry Garcia,' a cross of Martha W. with an unnamed Paeonia delavayi hybrid. On its own it grows as an ordinary, dependable garden lactiflora rather than a show-quality exhibition peony. Plant in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and leave the crown undisturbed once established, since peonies resent frequent transplanting.
sources: American Peony Society Peony Registry — Martha W.
